court: Office of Hearings and Appeals — Director's Decisions (U.S. Dept. of the Interior)
title: 26 OHA 31 — IN RE SANDERFORD
text:
November 7, 2003
IN THE MATTER OF : Docket No. D 2003-34
JANE SANDERFORD :
: Waiver Appeal
:
: Request for Reconsideration
: Denied
ORDER
On October 9, 2003, Ms. Jane Sanderford filed a petition for reconsideration
pursuant to 344 DM 9.6C (1998) of the Ad Hoc Board of Appeals September 17,
2003, decision styled In the Matter of Jane Sanderford, 25 OHA 257 (2003). The
Board’s decision affirmed the denial by the Payroll Operations Division (POD),
National Business Center, Office of the Secretary, Denver Colorado, of
Ms. Sanderford’s request for waiver of salary overpayment in the amount of
$1,788.75 as identified in Bill for Collection No. Q2760014585. Ms. Sanderford,
an employee of the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), had sought a waiver under
the provisions of 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000).
In its Administrative Report, POD 2002-285, prepared on December 5, 2002,
POD set forth the circumstances surrounding the overpayment of salary as follows:
Jane Sanderford, an employee of the Bureau of Land Management
(BLM), received erroneous overpayment when her award was input
with the incorrect amount. The award was to be for $2,500.00 and was
input as $5000.00.
(Administrative Report POD 2002-285, at 1).
26 OHA 31

D 2003-34
The Administrative Report included a summary of a letter from BLM in which
BLM explained that the amount to be paid to Ms. Sanderford was the topic of two
conversations between the BLM Personnel Specialist and the BLM Supervisory, Realty
Specialist. During the first conversation, the Personnel Specialist informed the
Supervisory, Realty Specialist that the amount of the award would be $5,000.00
instead of $2,500.00. However, during the second conversation, the Personnel
Specialist informed the Supervisory, Realty Specialist that the amount of the award
would not be $5,000.00. BLM noted that Ms. Sanderford was not informed of these
conversations. BLM stated that several weeks after these conversations,
Ms. Sanderford received a $5,000.00 award.
In her waiver request dated October 9, 2002, Ms. Sanderford provided the
following reasons in support of her request:
I relocated to the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), Las Vegas Field
Office, Nevada, in November, 2001. As a result of that permanent
change of station and the successful sale of my private residence, I was
entitled to receive a Star Award in the amount of $2,500.00. I filed the
appropriate paperwork to obtain the monetary award of $2,500.00. It
was signed by my Supervisor and forwarded to the appropriate office at
the Nevada State Office (NSO) in Reno, Nevada, for processing. During
the approval process it was noted that the amount of this award
payment had been increased to $5,000.00 per BLM Washington Office
IM #2002-175. I was not aware of this change at the time I filed the
paperwork for the award. Any change to the amount of the award
submitted was made by someone other than me.
(Waiver Request at 1).
Ms. Sanderford explained that the overpayment was the result of an
administrative error caused by someone who decided that based on Instruction
Memorandum (IM) No. 2002-175 she should be given a $5,000.00 award rather
than a $2,500.00 award. She emphasized that the overpayment was not the result
of any action on her part.
By letter dated December 9, 2002, POD informed Ms. Sanderford that her
waiver request had been denied. On appeal, Ms. Sanderford asserted that the letter
denying her waiver request failed to address the applicable rules pertaining to the
26 OHA 32

D 2003-34
amount of the award in regard to IM No. 2002-175. She pointed out that the award
was specifically linked to the sale of her home and that IM No. 2002-175 increased
the amount of such awards from $2,500.00 to $5,000.00. Therefore, she believed
that the $5,000.00 award was proper.
By decision dated September 17, 2003, this Board affirmed POD’s denial of
Ms. Sanderford’s waiver request pursuant to 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000) which authorizes
OHA to waive claims for overpayment of pay if collection would be contrary to equity
and good conscience and not in the best interests of the United States. This authority
may not be exercised if there is an indication of fraud, misrepresentation, fault, or
lack of good faith by the employee or any other person having an interest in
obtaining a waiver of the claim. See 344 DM 9 (1998). In our decision, we found
that Ms. Sanderford was not without fault in this matter because the record
demonstrated that she was aware of the overpayment. Ms. Sanderford stated in her
waiver request that she filed the appropriate paperwork to obtain the award of
$2,500.00. We found that when she received an award in the amount of $5,000.00,
rather than $2,500.00, she should have known that there had been an overpayment
and inquired as to the accuracy of the amount. We affirmed POD’s denial of
Ms. Sanderford’s waiver request based on the following:
Comptroller General decisions have held that if a reasonable person
would have inquired about the correctness of a payment, but the
employee did not, then the employee is not free from fault and the
claim may not be waived. Simon B. Guedea, B-189385, Aug. 10, 1977,
and cases cited. In these circumstances, it is clear that when
Ms. Sanderford received the $5,000.00 award, she knew that an over-
payment had occurred because she filed the paperwork for a $2,500.00
award. Where an employee was aware of the overpayment when it occurred,
a request for waiver will be denied. As a reasonable and prudent person who
knows that she is being overpaid, Ms. Sanderford should have set aside the
amount of overpayment for eventual refunding. In re Linda C. Mazzu,
17 OHA 108 (1999); Gilbert G. Quintero, B-183558, April 23, 1975. While
ideally no errors would occur in the payment process, such mistakes do occur
and Ms. Sanderford is not entitled to a windfall as a result.
In re Jane Sanderford, supra at 262.
26 OHA 33

D 2003-34
In her request for reconsideration, Ms. Sanderford referred to IM No. 2002-
175 dated May 20, 2002, and effective upon receipt. Attachment 1 to IM No. 2002-
175 provides answers to “Bureau of Land Management Permanent Change of Station
Frequently Asked Questions.” Provision No. 2 of Section II: Relocation Services
Contract states that a cash incentive award is available to an employee if the
employee sells his/her home without using the Relocation Services Contract.
Provision No. 2 provides that “[t]he State/Center Director will approve payment of
the cash incentive. The maximum relocation award amount is $5,000, and is raised
from $2,500 by this Instruction Memorandum.” Ms. Sanderford argued that at the
time she received her award, she was “in receipt” of IM No. 2002-175, and that it was
therefore reasonable for her to assume that the administrative office “had applied the
rule appropriately” as stated in IM No. 2002-175 and awarded her $5,000.00.
Ms. Sanderford stated that upon receipt of the award, she openly discussed the
award amount with her supervisors.
Ms. Sanderford asked that the Board consider the following two points:
First, was the rule properly applied or did I receive an incorrect
amount? Secondly, given that I was in receipt of the new instruction
memorandum, was it reasonable to assume the payment I received was
accurate. If I reasonably believed the payment was accurate, I request
acceptance of my waiver request.
(Request for Reconsideration, at 1).
In response to the first point, we note as we did in our September 17, 2003,
decision that it is not within the Board’s jurisdiction to interpret IM No. 2002-175
and to determine whether it was properly applied in Ms. Sanderford’s case. If
Ms. Sanderford was disputing the amount of her award, the matter would have been
properly considered pursuant to the Debt Collection Act of 1982, 5 U.S.C. § 5514
(2000). Under the provisions of 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000), OHA has authority to waive
an employee’s liability for debts arising from erroneous payments of pay, certain
allowances, and travel and transportation expenses when collection would be against
equity and good conscience and not in the best interests of the United States. This
waiver authority, however, applies only to claims arising out of “erroneous
payments.”
26 OHA 34

D 2003-34
If Ms. Sanderford believed that the $5,000.00 payment to her was the result of
administrative error as she indicated in her waiver request, then we have authority to
consider the matter under the waiver provisions as we did in our September 17,
2003, decision. In regard to her second point, Ms. Sanderford questioned whether it
was reasonable for her to assume that the $5,000.00 payment was accurate in light of
the fact that she had received a copy of the new instruction memorandum. Under the
circumstances, we find that it was not reasonable for Ms. Sanderford to make this
assumption. The attachment to IM No. 2002-175 provides that the maximum
relocation award amount is $5,000.00. Under this provision, Ms. Sanderford could
have been awarded any amount up to and including $5,000.00. When she received
the $5,000.00 payment instead of the $2,500.00 award for which she had filed, she
should have inquired as to whether the $5,000.00 amount was correct. Although
Ms. Sanderford stated that after receiving the award she openly discussed the amount
of the award with her supervisors, she did not state that she was told that the
$5,000.00 payment was correct. It was not reasonable for her to assume that the
$5,000.00 payment was correct based on IM No. 2002-175 without confirming this
assumption with her personnel office. See In re James D. Ration, 23 OHA 150, 153
(2003). Therefore, we find that Ms. Sanderford is not without fault in this matter,
and Bill for Collection No. Q2760014585 in the amount of $1,788.75 may not be
waived.
The general rules relating to procedures and practice before OHA are codified
at 43 CFR Part 4, Subpart B (2001). In order to be entitled to reconsideration of a
decision of an Ad Hoc Board, a petitioner is required by 43 CFR 4.21(d) (2001) to
show that "sufficient reason" exists for the Board to reconsider its decision, also
demonstrating that there exist "extraordinary circumstances" which justify reconsider-
ation. Under the standards and procedures for waivers set forth at 344 DM 9 (1998),
the request for reconsideration must demonstrate that the Director of OHA has
committed a material error of law or policy. 344 DM 9.6C (1998). After carefully
considering Ms. Sanderford’s petition for reconsideration, we conclude that she has
failed to demonstrate that sufficient reason and extraordinary circumstances exist for
reconsidering the Board's September 17, 2003, decision; nor has she shown that
there has been a material error of law or policy in this instance.
26 OHA 35

D 2003-34
Therefore, pursuant to the authority delegated to this Ad Hoc Board of Appeals
by the Secretary of the Interior, 43 CFR 4.1, Ms. Sanderford’s petition to reconsider
the Board's September 17, 2003, decision affirming POD’s denial of Ms. Sanderford’s
waiver request is denied. The Board’s decision constitutes the final administrative
determination by the Department in this matter. 344 DM 9 (1998).
